messages.subject: Problems running a model
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I'm having a problem to run a INLA model with R.
I will describe what I was trying and I will really appreciate any help.

First of all, I load a shp file which can be downloaded here: https://geoftp.ibge.gov.br/organizacao_do_territorio/estrutura_territorial/amazonia_legal/2021/Mun_Amazonia_Legal_2021_shp.zip

With the command:
map = st_read('Mun_Amazonia_Legal_2021.shp').

I've changed the map colnames from CD_MUN and AREA_TOT to codMunRes and areaTot (if you want to run the code).

So, with my data, which I called test_df:

I did a join with the map object with:
test_df_map = map |> inner_join(test_df, by = 'codMunRes')

to guarantee that both objects had the same cities.

After that, I used the pmatch function to make an useful ID to R-INLA:
test_df$area = pmatch(
 test_df$codMunRes,
 test_df_map$codMunRes
)

omit the NAs:
test_df = test_df |> na.omit()

and the output was:

With it, I tried to create the graph file:
temp = poly2nb(test_df_map)
nb2INLA('amazon.graph', temp)

path = 'amazon.graph'

and tried to fit the model:
formula = numCasos ~ 1 + f(area, model = 'bym2', graph = path)
inla(formula = formula, family = 'poisson', data = test_df,
 control.compute = list(cpo = T, dic = T, waic = T),
 verbose = T)

that returned me the following error:

Anyone has any idea?

Thanks for the attention.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Number of threads warning when running
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Number of threads warning when running
messages.body_plain:
You may run an older version?  With R-4.2 the most recent testing
version is  INLA_23.01.31

anyway, the argument should work (works for me), but the new general
format is

inla.setOption(num.threads="A:B")

where A is the number of threads in the outher layer and B (default=1)
is in the inner layer, see

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.04678.pdf

this works best when the PARDISO library is enabled; see

	inla.pardiso()

so you could set

	inla.setOption(num.threads="8")

messages.subject: How big is big with inla.mode="experimental" ? (#observations)
messages.subject_clean: How big is big with inla.mode="experimental" ? (#observations)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have read on the forum that using  inla.mode="experimental"  can speed up the calculations and make the run time less dependent on the number of observations.

But how big is big? Are we talking about millions or billions or trillions of observations? Perhaps it depends on the computational resources available, but some guidelines would be helpful. I need to convince some people that INLA can be used with many observations...

Best
Fredrik

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] missing readShapePoly function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Since the whole maptools and rgdal packages are deprecated and being retired this year, you’ll need to modify code to use sf instead (the sp package will still work, but  it will call sf internally, so it’s safer to do that directly where possible).
sf::st_read() seems to be the closest replacement to readShapePoly, but the syntax will be different.
poly2nb is part of the spdep package, so you may need to check the documentation for that as well.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] About spatio-temporal models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I did not see a spatiotemporal term in your model, I only saw a spatial and a temporal term.

There are 3 ways to inform about Population/Exposure for a Poisson likelihood in INLA. Suppose you have a column logPop which is the log of the population:
  adding offset in the formula such as + offset(logPop)
  specifying it as exposure, inla(..., E = population)
  using the offset argument, inla(..., offset = logPop)
notice that when you specify it using the Exposure (E = ...) then your fitted values are in the relative risk scale.

Best regards,
Elias

samples=inla.posterior.sample(n=nsamp, result=m1, selection = list(Predictor=33))

predictor.samples=unlist(lapply(samples, function(x)(x$latent[1])))

For the hyperparameter:
hyper.samples=unlist(lapply(samples, function(x)(x$hyperpar[1])))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

if the memory use for storing enough full samples is the limiting
factor, then I would suggest a block-wise approach; generate samples,
compute/simulate the functional you want, and either store just those
values, or if all you want are posterior mean&var or similar summary,
accumulate the information needed to compute those from multiple block
samples.  This technique can also be used for quantiles, by using
recursive quantile estimators (I've been working towards an
implementation of that, for use cases like this).

Finn

Hi everyone,

When reading this post (https://punama.github.io/BDI_INLA/), I found a computationally cheaper method for prediction as follows:

#create the spatial structure
sfield_nodes <- model$summary.random$spatial.field['mean']
field <- (Aprediction %*% as.data.frame(sfield_nodes)[, 1])

#make empty matrix to fill predictions
pred <- matrix(NA, nrow = dim(Aprediction)[1], ncol = 1)

## Calculate Predicted values using regression formula
pred <- model$summary.fixed['Intercept', 'mean'] +
  model$summary.fixed['Access', 'mean'] * Access +
  model$summary.fixed['Elevation', 'mean'] * Elevation +
  model$summary.fixed['EVI', 'mean'] * EVI +
  model$summary.fixed['LST_day', 'mean'] * LST_day +
  field

# write results in csv
results <- exp(pred)/(1+exp(pred))

the code uses the mean of the fixed and random coefficience to calculate the mean predictor and then tranforms it to the respose scale using a inverse link function.  I was wondering how to obtain the 95% credible interval and sd of the response-scale prediction. Thanks very much.

steven

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] About spatio-temporal models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The use of expected counts (according to demographic or just a base reference rate) is to have the interpretation of the model terms as log of relative risk (relative to how you computed the expected number of counts).

To help with zero-inflation the last thing I would do is to use the zero-inflated-likelihood models, like the zeroinflatedpoisson or zeroinflatednegativebinomial likelihoods. Before this I would try to incorporate in the model the mechanism causing the (marginal) zero inflation. Usually the marginal zero inflation is due to something causing the rate to vary. Once you condition on it you both solve the problem and model it. For example, some diseases have a temporal cycle and then a model term capturing it is the sensible thing to include in the model.

In a lot of cases once you explain the mean well you do not need to worry about the variance ;)

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] query about prediction using computationally cheaper method
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

When you fit the model for the observed data you can ask inla() to return the configurations. Then you can use the inla.posterior.sample() to draw samples and compute what you have computed with the posterior mean of each model term for each sample drawn. Then you can compute credible intervals, or some other functional, with these samples. This is easier if you use the inlabru package as illustrated here: https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/random_fields_2d.html

Elias

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is the marginal distribution of the response variable important?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is the marginal distribution of the response variable important?
messages.body_plain:
The marginal distribution of the response variables isn't directly
modelled, and it depends on if you're looking at some subset of the
data, etc; only the conditional distributions are modelled.

But if you apply different scaling on different subgroups of the
response variable, you're changing the corresponding conditional
distributions as well, so whether that changes the theoretical model
or not depends on if you incorporate that scaling information directly
into the model as well. E.g. if you have the grouping as a individual
shifts (intercepts or random effects) per group and different
variances in each group.

Finn

On Tue, 7 Feb 2023 at 16:25, JJ Hubbard <jordanj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Is there ever a situation where INLA might be sensitive to the marginal distribution of the response and we would want to transform it? Or is the fitting process nearly/totally independent of f_Y(y)?

In theory, no, in practice, yes.
In theory, one can always scale (continuous) responses and compensate
for that by changing the priors in a corresponding way, and nothing
really changes.
In practice, there are numerical considerations, so that the
calculations are more numerically stable for values around 0/1 than
around 1 million, say.

> Finn, when you say "have the grouping as a individual shifts (intercepts or random effects)" do you mean have a random effect identifying which group an observation belongs to, or including the mean/standard deviation used for scaling as a predictor?

The former. But the latter could be used to exactly compensate for the
scaling. But this has nothing to do with inla really, and is a
fundamental part of the mathematics behind all
mathematical/statistical models. inla just provides a way to specify
(a subset of) models.

Finn

>
> On Tuesday, February 7, 2023 at 8:11:37 AM UTC-8 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is the marginal distribution of the response variable important?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is the marginal distribution of the response variable important?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
No, the marginal distribution for y is a complicated mixture distribution and only rarely has any special form, as it depends on the distribution of covariate values etc, etc,etc. it’s a classic error to act as if it should follow some simple model; in regression models, it’s the conditional observation distributions that one makes assumptions for, not the marginal data distribution.

Finn

> Hi,
>
> When you fit the model for the observed data you can ask inla() to return the configurations. Then you can use the inla.posterior.sample() to draw samples and compute what you have computed with the posterior mean of each model term for each sample drawn. Then you can compute credible intervals, or some other functional, with these samples. This is easier if you use the inlabru package as illustrated here: https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/random_fields_2d.html

Em terça-feira, 7 de fevereiro de 2023 às 03:58:46 UTC-3, eliask...@gmail.com escreveu:
> Hi,
>
> The use of expected counts (according to demographic or just a base reference rate) is to have the interpretation of the model terms as log of relative risk (relative to how you computed the expected number of counts).
>
> To help with zero-inflation the last thing I would do is to use the zero-inflated-likelihood models, like the zeroinflatedpoisson or zeroinflatednegativebinomial likelihoods. Before this I would try to incorporate in the model the mechanism causing the (marginal) zero inflation. Usually the marginal zero inflation is due to something causing the rate to vary. Once you condition on it you both solve the problem and model it. For example, some diseases have a temporal cycle and then a model term capturing it is the sensible thing to include in the model.
>
> In a lot of cases once you explain the mean well you do not need to worry about the variance ;)
>
> best regards,
> Elias
>
> On Tue, 7 Feb 2023 at 02:36, Moisés Augusto <moise...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Kay, I'll try it.
> > My data is zero inflated. I read that in that cases, use the expected counts would not be great. Is this wrong?
> > Em segunda-feira, 6 de fevereiro de 2023 às 09:40:08 UTC-3, eliask...@gmail.com escreveu:
> > > ... modeling the relative risk is usually better (than the rate case/person that seems to be what you are trying) and all you have to do is to compute the expected value. If the disease you are considering does not have specific rates depending on age or gender (or some demographic factor), then to compute the expected value is easier as it simplifies to
> > >      expected = population * sum(y) / sum(population)
> > > which you can supply in the E argument of inla()
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mon, 6 Feb 2023 at 15:35, Elias T. Krainski <eliask...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > I did not see a spatiotemporal term in your model, I only saw a spatial and a temporal term.
> > > >
> > > > There are 3 ways to inform about Population/Exposure for a Poisson likelihood in INLA. Suppose you have a column logPop which is the log of the population:
> > > >   adding offset in the formula such as + offset(logPop)
> > > >   specifying it as exposure, inla(..., E = population)
> > > >   using the offset argument, inla(..., offset = logPop)
> > > > notice that when you specify it using the Exposure (E = ...) then your fitted values are in the relative risk scale.
> > > >
> > > > Best regards,
> > > > Elias
> > > >
> > > >

When using inla.stack, it's really only the APredictor you should
access directly (unless you know the details of the internal model
representation), and the indexing into APredictor is the order that
you specified your predictor;
use inla.stack.index(stack, tag = ...) to find out which indices of
APredictor correspond to a specific sub-stack with a given tag.

Finn

messages.subject: Heteroskedastic Gaussian Regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Two Questions:

I was recently just reading the INLA review from Martino, and in the closing section of the paper, she states that by nesting INLA within MCMC, it is possible to estimate the dependence of the mean and variance of a Gaussian likelihood on a set of covariates. Doesn't that open up the possibility to compute distributional (GAMLSS) type models? Has this been done?

Within the scope of GAMLSS models, the standard method (for Gaussian Models) iterates between the mean and variance estimates. The preliminary mean fit is used to generate variance estimates which are fitted to, and then the fitted variances are used in a weighted regression. The previous steps are repeated till convergence. Are there analogous schemes using INLA?

Best,

WW

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Short answer: we developed the inlabru interface partly to make this easier for spatial model than hand-coding the stack usage, and to make general prediction with posterior samples easier. The generate() and predict() methods, together with the component and bru_mapper systems takes care of the needed mappings.
See the spatial examples on the inlabru GitHub.I’m pages (see link from inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org>)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Heteroskedastic Gaussian Regression
messages.body_plain:
Yes,
With the inlabru interface you can specify predictor expressions like
  ~ something + exp(otherthing) * randomeffect
that has that kind of effect, and inlabru uses iterated inla on successive predictor linearisation to estimate it. (Arbitrary R expressions are allowed, so the system is _very_ general, and limited mostly by what can be imagined, and by what leads to well defined unimodal posterior distributions.)

Finn

The preliminary mean fit is used to generate variance estimates which are fitted to, and then the fitted variances are used in a weighted regression. The previous steps are repeated till convergence. Are there analogous schemes using INLA?

messages.subject_clean: Need help understaning INLA SPDE code and results
messages.body_plain:
I am a newbie to SPDE modeling and am trying hard to learn how to use R_INLA to fit a spatial SPDE model including multiple fixed effects and a single fixed effect measured with error by studying the example of Section 3.2 in Kranski et al. 2019 Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA.  I am hoping
that someone can help me to better understand some of the code, the contents
of the resulting inla-class object.  Complete working code is listed below
my following questions:

1. Below the block for dat0, the data stack (stk.0) includes "x0" and "x0w"
   in the list of effects.  x0 is simply 1:n.x and x0w is a vector of ones. What is the purpose of those, and how would one know to include them in the data stack?

    2. hfix and pprec are defined lists that are included in control.family in the
call to inla(). hfix seems to define the hyperprior for the fixed effect (x). I have moderately informative priors for the fixed effects in my real data. What could than also be accomplished using control.fixed? If not, then can the hyperpriors for any and all fixed effect be defined and fed to control.family?

    3. In the resulting inla-class object res, res$summary.hyperpar includes
rows with the names "Precision for the Gaussian observations" and "Precision for the Gaussian observations[2]" The summaries for the tow are very different. The second contains the desired information. Why are there these two sets of precisions?

    4. I am interested in producing summaries and maps of the unknown fixed effect x, which is modeled using the 2nd likelihood.  The values of x _seem_ to be in
res$marginals.random$x. Is that correct?  How can one extract summaries of those values at both the sampling locations and obtain predicted values at all of the vertices of the mesh?  The task looks similar to the code under "imagemv" in the following code, but it is not clear to me how to get the summaries of x.

5. Following on Q4, how can one re-associate index values for the sampling locations in the inla-class object and the mesh verticies with the spatial coordinates for graphing?

I am sincerely grateful for any help I can get.

Best regards,
Steve Gutreuter
sgutr...@gmail.com

#################################################################
## Matern SPDE measurement error model, Section 3.2 in
## Krainski ET, Gómez-Rubio V, Bakka H, Lenzi A, Castro-Camilo D, Simpson D,
##    Lindgren F, Rue H. Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial
##    Differential Equations Using R and INLA. CRC Press, 2019.
#################################################################
library(INLA)
library(knitr)
library(fields)
library(viridisLite)
library(RColorBrewer)
#################################################################
## Helper functions
#################################################################
book.rMatern <- function(n, coords, sigma=1, range, kappa = sqrt(8*nu)/range, variance = sigma^2, nu=1) {
    m <- as.matrix(dist(coords))
    m <- exp((1-nu)*log(2) + nu*log(kappa*m)-
             lgamma(nu))*besselK(m*kappa, nu)
    diag(m) <- 1
    return(drop(crossprod(chol(variance*m),
                          matrix(rnorm(nrow(coords)*n), ncol=n))))
}
book.plot.field <- function(field, mesh, projector, xlim, ylim,
                dims=c(300,300), poly, asp = 1,
                axes = FALSE, xlab = '', ylab = '',
                col = book.color.c(), ...){
  if (missing(mesh)) {
    if (missing(projector)) {
      if (missing(xlim) | missing(ylim)) {
        image.plot(field, asp = asp, axes = axes,
                   xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, col = col, ...)
      } else {
        image.plot(field, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, asp = asp,
                   axes = axes, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, col = col, ...)
      }
    } else {
      if (missing(xlim)) xlim <- range(projector$x)
      if (missing(ylim)) ylim <- range(projector$y)
      field.proj <- inla.mesh.project(projector, field)
      image.plot(x = projector$x, y = projector$y, z = field.proj,
                 asp=asp, axes=axes, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab,
                 col=col, xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim, ...)
    }
  } else {
    if (missing(xlim)) xlim <- range(mesh$loc[,1])
    if (missing(ylim)) ylim <- range(mesh$loc[,2])
    projector <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim = xlim,
                                     ylim = ylim, dims=dims)
    field.proj <- inla.mesh.project(projector, field)
    image.plot(x = projector$x, y = projector$y, z = field.proj,
               asp=asp, axes=axes, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, col=col, ...)
  }
  if (!missing(poly))
      plot(poly, add = TRUE, col = 'grey')
}
book.color.c = function(n = 201) {
  return(viridis(n))
}
#################################################################
## Example from Section 3.2
#################################################################
## ----simloc0-------------------------------------------------------------
n.x <- 70
n.y <- 50
set.seed(1)
loc.y <- cbind(runif(n.y) * 10, runif(n.y) * 5)
loc.x <- cbind(runif(n.x) * 10, runif(n.x) * 5)

n.x <- nrow(loc.x)
n.y <- nrow(loc.y)

## ----simloc----
par(mar=c(2.5, 2.5, 0.5, 0.5), mgp=c(1.5, 0.5, 0))
plot(loc.x, pch = 19, col = gray(0.5), asp = 1, xlab = '', ylab = '')
points(loc.y, pch = 17)

## ----simula--------------------------------------------------------------
range.v <- 3
sigma.v <- 0.5
range.m <- 3
sigma.m <- 1
set.seed(2)
v <- book.rMatern(n = 1, coords = loc.y, range = range.v,
  sigma = sigma.v, nu = 1)
m <- book.rMatern(n = 1, coords = rbind(loc.x, loc.y),
  range = range.m, sigma = sigma.m, nu = 1)

## ----params--------------------------------------------------------------
alpha.y <- 2
alpha.x <- 5
beta.x <- 0.3
sigma.e <- 0.2

## ----simxw0--------------------------------------------------------------
x.x <- alpha.x + m[1:n.x]
w.x <- x.x + rnorm(n.x, 0, sigma.e)
x.y <- alpha.x + m[n.x + 1:n.y]
w.y <- x.y + rnorm(n.y, 0, sigma.e)

## ----simxw----
par(mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 0.5, 0.5), mgp = c(1.5, 0.5, 0))
plot(c(w.x, w.y), c(x.x, x.y), xlab = 'w', ylab = 'x')
abline(c(0, 1))

## ----simy----------------------------------------------------------------
eta.y <- alpha.y + beta.x * x.y + v
set.seed(3)
yy <- rpois(n.y, exp(eta.y))

## ----mesh----------------------------------------------------------------
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(rbind(loc.x, loc.y),
  max.edge = min(range.m, range.v) * c(1 / 3, 1),
  offset = min(range.m, range.v) * c(0.5, 1.5))
cat(paste0("Number of vertices: ",  mesh$n, "\n"))
plot(mesh)
## ----Apred---------------------------------------------------------------
Ax <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = loc.x)
Ay <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = loc.y)
dim(Ax) ; dim(Ay)
## ----spde----------------------------------------------------------------
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(0.5, 0.01), # P(practic.range < 0.5) = 0.01
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)) # P(sigma > 1) = 0.01

## ----dat0----------------------------------------------------------------
stk.0 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(Y = cbind(rep(0, n.y), NA, NA)),
  A = list(1, Ay),
  effects = list(data.frame(alpha.x = 1, x0 = 1:n.y, x0w = -1),
    m = 1:spde$n.spde),
  tag = 'dat.0')

## ----datx----------------------------------------------------------------
stk.x <- inla.stack(
  data = list(Y = cbind(NA, w.x, NA)),
  A = list(1, Ax),
  effects = list(alpha.x = rep(1, n.x), m = 1:mesh$n),
  tag = 'dat.x')

## ----daty----------------------------------------------------------------
stk.y <- inla.stack(
  data = list(Y = cbind(NA, NA, yy)),
  A = list(1, Ay),
  effects = list(data.frame(alpha.y = 1, x = 1:n.y),
    v = 1:mesh$n),
  tag = 'dat.y')

## ----formula-------------------------------------------------------------
form <- Y ~  0 + alpha.x + alpha.y +
  f(m, model = spde) + f(v, model = spde) +
  f(x0, x0w, model = 'iid',
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = -20, fixed = TRUE))) +
  f(x, copy = 'x0', fixed = FALSE,
    hyper = list(theta = list(prior='normal', param = c(0, 1))))

## ----hfix----------------------------------------------------------------
hfix <- list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = 20,
  fixed = TRUE)))

## ----pprec---------------------------------------------------------------
pprec <- list(hyper = list(theta = list(prior = 'pc.prec',
  param=c(0.2, 0.5))))

## ----fit-----------------------------------------------------------------
stk <- inla.stack(stk.0, stk.x, stk.y)
res <- inla(form, data = inla.stack.data(stk),
  family = c('gaussian', 'gaussian', 'poisson'),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,
    A = inla.stack.A(stk)),
  control.family = list(hfix, pprec, list()))

## ----resfix, echo = FALSE------------------------------------------------
## Add estimates of fixed effects ahd hyperparameters
tab.s <- rbind(res$summary.fixed[, c(1, 2, 3, 5)],
  res$summary.hyperpar[, c(1, 2, 3, 5)])
sigma.e.mar <- inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1 / sqrt(exp(x)),
  res$internal.marginals.hy[[2]])
tab.s[3, ] <- unlist(inla.zmarginal(sigma.e.mar, silent = TRUE))[c(1, 2, 3, 7)]
tab.s <- cbind(
  Parameter = c("$\\alpha_x$", "$\\alpha_y$", "$\\sigma_{\\epsilon}$",
    rownames(res$summary.hyperpar)[-c(1,2)]),
  True = c(alpha.x, alpha.y, sigma.e, range.m, sigma.m, range.v,
    sigma.v, beta.x),
  tab.s[-4,])
names(tab.s) <- c("Parameter", "True", "Mean",
  "St. Dev.", "2.5\\% quant.", "97.5\\% quant.")
## ----label = "tabresfix", echo = FALSE-----------------------------------
knitr::kable(tab.s,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Summary of the posterior densities of model parameters.",
  format = "pandoc")

## ----regparsm----
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 3), mgp = c(3, 1, 0))
plot(res$marginals.fixed[[1]], type = 'l',
     xlab = expression(alpha[x]), ylab = 'Density')
abline(v = alpha.x, col = "red")

plot(res$marginals.fixed[[2]], type = 'l',
     xlab = expression(alpha[y]), ylab = 'Density')
abline(v = alpha.y, col = "red")

plot(res$marginals.hyperpar[[6]], type = 'l',
     xlab = expression(beta), ylab = 'Density')
abline(v = beta.x, col = "red")

plot(sigma.e.mar, type = 'l',
     xlab = expression(sigma[u]), ylab = 'Density')
abline(v = sigma.e, col = "red")
## ----rfparsme----
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 0.1, 0.5), mgp = c(1.5, 0.5, 0))
for (j in 3:6) {
  ii <- res$marginals.hyperpar[[j]][,2] > sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
  plot(res$marginals.hyperpar[[j]], type = 'l',
    xlim = range(res$marginals.hyperpar[[j]][ii, 1]),
    xlab = names(res$marginals.hyperpar)[j], ylab = 'Density')
  abline(v = c(range.m, sigma.m, range.v, sigma.v)[j - 2], col = "red")
}
## ----predm---------------------------------------------------------------
mesh2locs <- rbind(Ax, Ay)
m.mu <http://m.mu> <- drop(mesh2locs %*% res$summary.ran$m$mean)
m.sd <http://m.sd> <- drop(mesh2locs %*% res$summary.ran$m$sd)

## ----prdplotme----
par(mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 0.5, 0.5), mgp = c(1.5, 0.5, 0))
plot(m.mu <http://m.mu>, m, asp = 1, type = 'n',
  xlab = 'Predicted', ylab = 'Simulated')
segments(m.mu <http://m.mu> - 2 * m.sd <http://m.sd>, m, m.mu <http://m.mu> + 2 * m.sd <http://m.sd>, m,
  lty = 2, col = gray(0.75))
abline(c(0, 1), col = 4)
points(m.mu <http://m.mu>, m, pch = 3, cex = 0.5)

## ----imagemv----------------------
# Create grid for projection
prj <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5))

# Settings for plotting device
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5),
  mgp = c(1.5, 0.5, 0))

# Posterior mean of 'm'
book.plot.field(field = res$summary.ran$m$mean, projector = prj)
points(loc.x, cex = 0.3 + (m - min(m))/diff(range(m)))
# Posterior mean of 'v'
book.plot.field(field = res$summary.ran$v$mean, projector = prj)
points(loc.y, cex = 0.3 + (v - min(v))/diff(range(v))

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a conceptual question about modeling space-time interactions. I am interested in how the prevalence of a particular fungus has changed over time within its plant hosts. I have data marking the presence/absence of this fungus in georeferenced museum specimens, which are host plants collected across the US over the last ~100 years.

I've been reading on the different types of interaction models but was having a hard time telling if there is a reason against including space time interactions as fixed effects with an SPDE model. To me, this model potentially would allow me to say what is the rate of change in the prevalence for each location, while treating space continuously.

1: formula(Y ~ 1 + year  + species:year:lat + year:lon + year:lat:lon + f(s, model = spde))

I've seen most of the examples include space-time interactions for areal data which I could, but feels like giving up some information.

2: formula(Y ~ 1 +  year + f(county, model = "bym") + f(county, year, model = "iid")

And then I've also seen lots of examples include some sort of temporal autocorrelation model, but also not commonly with an  SPDE.

3: formula(Y ~ 1 + f(s, model=spde, group = year, control.group=list(model="ar1"))

In general that makes sense to me, but it feels like the data, relatively few samples over time for each location, is a little bit limited to justify some sort of temporal model. I'm primarily interested in whether the rate of change is different in different locations rather than the spatial field for each year if that makes sense.  The examples and articles I've found have been very helpful, but struggle a bit to understand where certain types of interactions are "separable" or not and require constraints. Is there a reason why formula 1 would be inappropriate? I really appreciate any insights.

Thank you,
Josh Fowler

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Heteroskedastic Gaussian Regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

we're working on a paper that will have more information about inlabru
(there are a couple of papers available but they don't have all the
maths in them) but the vignette contains the fundamentals.

In

~ something + exp(otherthing) * randomeffect

the "something" part would the the linear predictor model, and
"exp(otherthing)" would be a log-linear model for the standard
deviation, and randomeffect the iid effect that would normally be part
of the observation model instead;
  bru(..., like(...,
control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=15,fixed=TRUE)))))
would be needed to fix the gaussian observation likelihood precision
to a large value.

Note that the "generalised linear models" technique of just specifying
mean and variance models isn't a complete probabilistic model, so in
any Bayesian context you have to construct your _entire_ model
probabilistically.
Once that's done, in some cases those can be written in inlabru or
INLA-able formats. In other cases not.

Finn

library(sp)
library(terra)
library(raster)
library(geodata)

boundaries <- getData(name = "GADM", country = "Portugal", level = 0)
## Removing the islands from the map
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
boundaries <- boundaries %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON") %>%
  mutate(area = st_area(.)) %>%
  arrange(desc(area)) %>%
  slice(1)

boundaries <- boundaries %>% st_transform(25830)

#PREPARING DATA ON NO2 LEVELS IN PORTUGAL

## Retrieving data

no2 <- read.csv("no2portavg.csv")
no2 <- no2[, c(
  "ReportingYear", "StationLocalId",
  "SamplingPoint_Longitude",
  "SamplingPoint_Latitude",
  "AQValue"
)]
names(no2) <- c("year", "id", "long", "lat", "value")

## Transforming the data to UTM projection

stations <- st_as_sf(data.frame(long = no2$long, lat = no2$lat),
                     coords = c("long", "lat"))
st_crs(stations) <- st_crs(4326)
stations <- stations %>% st_transform(25830)
no2[, c("x", "y")] <- st_coordinates(stations)

## Removing the islands from the NO2 data and plotting different visualizations
ind <- st_intersects(boundaries, stations)
no2 <- no2[ind[[1]], ]

# Constructing the mesh

library(INLA)
library(sf)
library(rgdal)

coo <- cbind(no2$x, no2$y)
bnd <- inla.nonconvex.hull(st_coordinates(boundaries)[, 1:2])
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  loc = coo, boundary = bnd,
  max.edge = c(100000, 200000), cutoff = 1000
)

# Building a SPDE model on the mesh

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE,
  prior.range = c(10000, 0.01), # P(range < 10000) = 0.01
  prior.sigma = c(3, 0.01) # P(sigma > 3) = 0.01
)

# Creating an index set

timesn <- length(unique(no2$year))
indexs <- inla.spde.make.index("s",
                               n.spde = spde$n.spde,
                               n.group = timesn
)

lengths(indexs)

#Projection matrix

group <- no2$year - min(no2$year) + 1
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coo, group = group)

#Prediction data

bb <- st_bbox(boundaries)
x <- seq(bb$xmin - 1, bb$xmax + 1, length.out = 50)
y <- seq(bb$ymin - 1, bb$ymax + 1, length.out = 50)
dp <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))

# Keeping only locations that coincide with Portugal's map:
stations <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = dp[, 1], y = dp[, 2]),
              coords = c("x", "y")
)
st_crs(stations) <- st_crs(25830)
ind <- st_intersects(boundaries, stations)
dp <- dp[ind[[1]], ]
plot(dp, asp = 1)

dp <- rbind(cbind(dp, 1), cbind(dp, 2), cbind(dp, 3), cbind(dp, 4), cbind(dp, 5), cbind(dp, 6), cbind(dp, 7))

coop <- dp[, 1:2]
groupp <- dp[, 3]
Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coop, group = groupp)

# Stacking the data for estimation and prediction

stk.e <- inla.stack(
  tag = "est",
  data = list(y = no2$value),
  A = list(1, A),
  effects = list(data.frame(b0 = rep(1, nrow(no2))), s = indexs)
)

stk.p <- inla.stack(
  tag = "pred",
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(1, Ap),
  effects = list(data.frame(b0 = rep(1, nrow(dp))), s = indexs)
)

stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.e, stk.p)

# Model formula

rprior <- list(theta = list(prior = "pccor1", param = c(0, 0.9)))

formula <- y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s,
                          model = spde, group = s.group,
                          control.group = list(model = "ar1", hyper = rprior)
)

# INLA call

res <- inla(formula,
            data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
            control.predictor = list(
              compute = TRUE,
              A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)
            ),
            verbose=TRUE

)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Context: I have presence-absence data over a large spatial area. In a non-spatial glm, my goal was to predict the probability of presence based on a number of geographical covariates. Once I had the "best" model after model selection, I would then use the resultant equation to predict the probability over a very fine grid located in a small portion of the original spatial area.

As my residuals had large spatial autocorrelation, I turned to INLA. However, I've been having issues with comprehension. I have three main questions:

1. Model selection
In standard GLM statistics, I would fit a model with fixed effects and the most probable interactions, then compare AIC and iteratively remove covariates until I have the best model. Then, I would use the final one to predict over a new area.
I had assumed this would be the case for INLA, but I am not sure. For example, I have INLA code that runs and successfully runs for the observation data. I then removed covariates and compared WAIC, and determined my "best" model.
Main question: Should I be following the standard model selection procedure for INLA in this way? Or does the inclusion of a prediction matrix mean I don't have to?
2. Observation data vs prediction data
My observational data is spread out over a very large spatial area (all of northern Myanmar), with ~5500 points (10:1 ratio of absence : presence). However, my prediction data is on a much finer grid. Specifically, it is 10 m resolution with 5.9 million pixels. I have the geographical covariate values for all the observational data points plus all the grid pixels.
To account for this, I ensured the mesh had a low cut-off (0.01), because 0.01 km = 10 m.
When trying to run INLA with the full prediction data, INLA would crash and say "Rerun with better starting values."  I tried specifying pcmatern mesh and priors, but that did not work.
However, when I tried using only a sample of the prediction data (2000 pixels vs all 5.9 million), the INLA run was successful.
Main question: Is the size difference between my observational data and prediction data contributing to INLA's crashing? It appears to be so.
3. inlabru
I had tried using inlabru because I thought that might help the crashing issues I was experiencing earlier. However, I found that when trying to use inlabru on just the observational data, it always crashes. I have included the code in the code snippet.
I thought I had translated the INLA code correctly to inlabru based on the vignettes and what I could understand from them.
Main question: Is there something I'm missing from the inlabru version of the code?

3. Code
I have attached sample code and the observational data plus a sample of the prediction data.
Thank you so much for your help / advice. This is very appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Advice for spatial INLA + binomial GLM model selection and troubleshooting
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Advice for spatial INLA + binomial GLM model selection and troubleshooting
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

1. To the extent that such model selection would be appropriate in a
frequentistic GLM setting, it would also be reasonable in a Bayesian
GLM setting.  From what I read nowadays it's a bit frowned upon also
in "standard" GLM settings (especially stepwise selection is very much
frowned upon).  But there are variations on these methods that can be
sensible in predictions settings where parameter inference isn't of
interest; keeping more covariates is only a problem if it makes
prediction worse. But to assess prediction fairly you'd need a
sensibly designed cross-validation approach, for example.  How to do
this appropriately is really an open research problem, and this isn't
tied to INLA, that just provides the calculations. It applies to _all_
spatial models.

2. Your prediction grid resolution shouldn't dictate your random field
component mesh resolution. The model mesh resolution only need to be
able to capture the spatial correlation; if that's estimated to ~100,
then the mesh resolution should be ok with being ~10.

3. In the inlabru code you don't just have a presence/absence Binomial
model, but also an LGCP likelihood, but there are no common components
between the two likelihoods, so it's unclear what the goal is. You're
also missing the samplers= argument, which makes it try to build a
model across the whole mesh, which is bound to be problematic when the
points onely cover parts of the domain.
If the fine resolution covariates had been involved, you'd have the
issue of needing an integration scheme fine enough to capture the
covariate values, and that's I guess where your idea of needing a very
fine mesh came from, although that would have needed to be applied to
the max.edge value, not the cutoff. However, that's unlikely to be
practical.
We have an ongoing research project on how to better deal with such
high resolution covariates for lgcp models.
For now, a better/safer approach is to smooth the covariates onto e.g.
the mesh used for the mySmooth model; local weighted averaging in some
form.

But for 3, I removed the lgcp part of the model and stepped into the
inlabru code, and there does appear to be some actual bug as well,
related to the "fixed" model, as somehow the entire model A-matrix has
become zero. I'll investigate.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
when you do 'inla.coxph' then its expanded into poisson regression, but the dimension of the model will depends on the data, as the expansion depends on it. this is why you get different dimensions in each fit.

looking at your code, it seems like you can benefite from having the baseline hazard defined on fixed intervals so you can more easily compare them, so I added

cut.points <- 1:30

and then use these 'cut.points' to define the baseline hazard

res.10 <- inla.coxph(inla.10 ~ 1 + time_std + inc_10_rate + as.factor(idzone),
data = c(list(inla.10 = inla.10, data0)),
control.hazard = list(cutpoints = cut.points))

res[[i]] <- inla(update(res.10$formula,
'. ~ . + f(idarea1, model = "bym2", graph = gFULL)'),

please use 'bym2' instead as it do automatically the right thing.

please check model/data as it seems that the information you have in the data is not to much for the model you have. maybe you want to merge it all and do the space-time model?

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Advice for spatial INLA + binomial GLM model selection and troubleshooting
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Advice for spatial INLA + binomial GLM model selection and troubleshooting
messages.body_plain:
Turns out there wasn't a bug in inlabru, but rather a mistake in the
model specification.
The "formula" is a general R expression, so when using the "fixed"
component construction for covariate interactions, only the name of
the combined "fixed" effect should be in the formula.
With that change, the code should run, although the issues around the
model specification for the "cp" part still apply.

fit <- bru(
  components = as.formula(compAll),
  inlabru::like(
    formula = coordinates ~ mySmooth,
    family = "cp",
    data = coordDF,
    domain = list(coordinates=mesh),
    include = c("mySmooth")
  ),
  inlabru::like(
    formula = dist ~ Intercept + mix,
    family = "binomial",
    data = as.data.frame(covars),
    exclude = c("mySmooth")
  ),
  options = list(
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
    control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")
  )
)

To help inlabru know it's a linear predictor, use ~ . and make sure
the include/exclude info is correct:
fit <- bru(
  components = as.formula(compAll),
  inlabru::like(
    formula = coordinates ~ .,
    family = "cp",
    data = coordDF,
    domain = list(coordinates=mesh),
    include = c("mySmooth")
  ),
  inlabru::like(
    formula = dist ~ .,
    family = "binomial",
    data = as.data.frame(covars),
    exclude = c("mySmooth")
  ),
  options = list(
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
    control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")
  )
)

Finn

On Fri, 10 Feb 2023 at 10:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> 1. To the extent that such model selection would be appropriate in a
> frequentistic GLM setting, it would also be reasonable in a Bayesian
> GLM setting.  From what I read nowadays it's a bit frowned upon also
> in "standard" GLM settings (especially stepwise selection is very much
> frowned upon).  But there are variations on these methods that can be
> sensible in predictions settings where parameter inference isn't of
> interest; keeping more covariates is only a problem if it makes
> prediction worse. But to assess prediction fairly you'd need a
> sensibly designed cross-validation approach, for example.  How to do
> this appropriately is really an open research problem, and this isn't
> tied to INLA, that just provides the calculations. It applies to _all_
> spatial models.
>
> 2. Your prediction grid resolution shouldn't dictate your random field
> component mesh resolution. The model mesh resolution only need to be
> able to capture the spatial correlation; if that's estimated to ~100,
> then the mesh resolution should be ok with being ~10.
>
> 3. In the inlabru code you don't just have a presence/absence Binomial
> model, but also an LGCP likelihood, but there are no common components
> between the two likelihoods, so it's unclear what the goal is. You're
> also missing the samplers= argument, which makes it try to build a
> model across the whole mesh, which is bound to be problematic when the
> points onely cover parts of the domain.
> If the fine resolution covariates had been involved, you'd have the
> issue of needing an integration scheme fine enough to capture the
> covariate values, and that's I guess where your idea of needing a very
> fine mesh came from, although that would have needed to be applied to
> the max.edge value, not the cutoff. However, that's unlikely to be
> practical.
> We have an ongoing research project on how to better deal with such
> high resolution covariates for lgcp models.
> For now, a better/safer approach is to smooth the covariates onto e.g.
> the mesh used for the mySmooth model; local weighted averaging in some
> form.
>
> But for 3, I removed the lgcp part of the model and stepped into the
> inlabru code, and there does appear to be some actual bug as well,
> related to the "fixed" model, as somehow the entire model A-matrix has
> become zero. I'll investigate.
>
> Finn
>
>
> On Thu, 9 Feb 2023 at 20:50, 'Ian McGregor' via R-inla discussion
> group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Context: I have presence-absence data over a large spatial area. In a non-spatial glm, my goal was to predict the probability of presence based on a number of geographical covariates. Once I had the "best" model after model selection, I would then use the resultant equation to predict the probability over a very fine grid located in a small portion of the original spatial area.
> >
> > As my residuals had large spatial autocorrelation, I turned to INLA. However, I've been having issues with comprehension. I have three main questions:
> >
> > 1. Model selection
> >
> > In standard GLM statistics, I would fit a model with fixed effects and the most probable interactions, then compare AIC and iteratively remove covariates until I have the best model. Then, I would use the final one to predict over a new area.
> > I had assumed this would be the case for INLA, but I am not sure. For example, I have INLA code that runs and successfully runs for the observation data. I then removed covariates and compared WAIC, and determined my "best" model.
> > Main question: Should I be following the standard model selection procedure for INLA in this way? Or does the inclusion of a prediction matrix mean I don't have to?
> >
> > 2. Observation data vs prediction data
> >
> > My observational data is spread out over a very large spatial area (all of northern Myanmar), with ~5500 points (10:1 ratio of absence : presence). However, my prediction data is on a much finer grid. Specifically, it is 10 m resolution with 5.9 million pixels. I have the geographical covariate values for all the observational data points plus all the grid pixels.
> > To account for this, I ensured the mesh had a low cut-off (0.01), because 0.01 km = 10 m.
> > When trying to run INLA with the full prediction data, INLA would crash and say "Rerun with better starting values."  I tried specifying pcmatern mesh and priors, but that did not work.
> > However, when I tried using only a sample of the prediction data (2000 pixels vs all 5.9 million), the INLA run was successful.
> > Main question: Is the size difference between my observational data and prediction data contributing to INLA's crashing? It appears to be so.
> >
> > 3. inlabru
> >
> > I had tried using inlabru because I thought that might help the crashing issues I was experiencing earlier. However, I found that when trying to use inlabru on just the observational data, it always crashes. I have included the code in the code snippet.
> > I thought I had translated the INLA code correctly to inlabru based on the vignettes and what I could understand from them.
> > Main question: Is there something I'm missing from the inlabru version of the code?
> >
> >
> > 3. Code
> >
> > I have attached sample code and the observational data plus a sample of the prediction data.
> >
> > Thank you so much for your help / advice. This is very appreciated!

On Thu, 2023-02-09 at 15:43 +0000, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi,
>
> we're working on a paper that will have more information about inlabru
> (there are a couple of papers available but they don't have all the
> maths in them) but the vignette contains the fundamentals.
>
> In
> ~ something + exp(otherthing) * randomeffect
> the "something" part would the the linear predictor model, and
> "exp(otherthing)" would be a log-linear model for the standard
> deviation, and randomeffect the iid effect that would normally be part
> of the observation model instead;
>   bru(..., like(...,
> control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(initial=15,fixed=TRUE)))))
> would be needed to fix the gaussian observation likelihood precision
> to a large value.
>
> Note that the "generalised linear models" technique of just specifying
> mean and variance models isn't a complete probabilistic model, so in
> any Bayesian context you have to construct your _entire_ model
> probabilistically.
> Once that's done, in some cases those can be written in inlabru or
> INLA-able formats. In other cases not.
>
> Finn
>
> On Thu, 9 Feb 2023 at 14:42, ww1124 <atri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hmm, I see. I am not (yet) familiar with the successive predictor
> > linearization. Do you have a reference for the method/idea behind it
> > (besides the inlabru vignette)?
> >
> > Was the idea roughly something to the effect of using the predictor
> > expression where I would specify a var(mu, ...) component in the
> > model as a function of the mean and other covariates and then use
> > that as a new weight in the regression? The var function would
> > estimate the variance and then specify a linear predictor to the
> > estimated variances to return a fitted weight for the regression?
> > So something like ~ (mu_effects)*1/var(mu, var_effects).
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > WW
> >
> > On Wednesday, February 8, 2023 at 6:59:07 PM UTC-5
> > finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > >
> > > Yes,
> > > With the inlabru interface you can specify predictor expressions
> > > like
> > >   ~ something + exp(otherthing) * randomeffect
> > > that has that kind of effect, and inlabru uses iterated inla on
> > > successive predictor linearisation to estimate it. (Arbitrary R
> > > expressions are allowed, so the system is _very_ general, and
> > > limited mostly by what can be imagined, and by what leads to well
> > > defined unimodal posterior distributions.)
> > >
> > > Finn

> > > and variance of a Gaussian likelihood on a set of covariates.
> > > Doesn't that open up the possibility to compute distributional

> > > Within the scope of GAMLSS models, the standard method (for

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you seem to have dropped the ~ - 1 part of the "fixed" component
input, you correctly had mix(~ -1 + ...) before.
However, before you only used it in the georeferenced part of the
model, where MatrixModels::model.Matrix(formula,data=.data.) works as
intended.
But for "cp" models, this use case wasn't really anticipated, and to
support automation, it might require a new method for accessing
spatial covariates may be needed.
I have an idea for it but will need time to consider it properly.

Currently, inlabru supports things like
  comp(covariate_raster, ..., main_layer = "name")
which ends up being evaluated as
  eval_spatial(covariate_raster, where = .data., layer = main_layer)
so it gets evaluated at the locations indicated by .data., which
includes the internal integration points.
But for
  comp(~ covar_name)
it just runs
  Matrix::Models::model.Matrix(~ covar_name, data = .data.)

So to handle your use case, it doesn't know how to set up the
likelihood automatically, as you don't know in advance where it will
want to evaluate the covariates.
This is nearly only a problem for model="fixed", and for spatial
covariates you could define new covariate rasters for the product
interactions and use as regular plain linear covariates instead,
so I'd suggest that as a workaround.
Instead of
  comp(~ -1 + a + b + a:b, model="fixed")
you'd need to do (if both a and b are layers in a covar raster):
  covar$ab <- covar$a * covar$b
(or something like that; it will be different for factor covariates;
make those into 0/1 dummy variables instead)
and in the components:
 ~ a(covar, main_layer="a") + b(covar, main_layer="b") + ab(covar,
main_layer="ab")

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm still new to INLA and trying to learn the ins and outs of the package. I need help with model convergence for an analysis I'm trying to run. I've looked all over the internet for help and solutions but cannot seem to figure it out, and I'm hoping someone here can help!

I have a very large dataset (~39 million individual-level observations) with ~845,000 cases (a prevalence of about 2%). I'm trying to run a rather complex mediation analysis, but I can't even get a very basic spatial logistic regression as outlined below to work:

base <- inla(y ~ x +
               f(re_u, model = "bym",
                 graph = g),
             family = "binomial", Ntrials = 1,
             data = df,
             control.predictor = list(link = 1))

I keep getting the following error/failure message.
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

I thought maybe it was due to my relatively rare outcome and unbalanced data. So, I resampled the noncases so that I would have a 9% prevalence in my dataset. I still get the same error and failure message. However, if I sample 10,000 cases and 100,000 non-cases so that my sample size is only 110,000 (but still a prevalence of 9%), the model converges just fine.

I'm not sure what the issue is once I add more observations. I've attached the output when I run the code on the larger dataset with verbose = TRUE. I tried adding inla(...safe = true) based on a response to another discussion thread here regarding the warning "GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=9221520" that shows up in the output, and the result is the same.

This analysis is for my dissertation, and I'm feeling really lost and hoping someone can point me in the right direction. I can't provide the data as it's a) huge and b) PHI. But I can provide an example dataset modeled after it if it's helpful.

I appreciate any advice!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] variance component with prior specifying non-zero floor
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] variance component with prior specifying non-zero floor
messages.body_plain:
It's a bit unclear, but I _think_ you're saying that you have prior
info that the _variance_ of an latent Gaussian iid component has a
plausible range (0.17, 0.23) ?

Then to specify a prior on the log-precision that respects that range
(with probability 95%, for example), then you could choose a prior
that gives a log-normal distribution on the precision with 0.025 and
0.975 quantiles of
(1/0.23, 1/0.17)
So the log-precision would need quantiles (log(1/0.23), log(1/0.17)).
That's fulfilled by having location parameter (log(1/0.23) +
log(1/0.17))/2 and standard deviation  (log(1/0.17) - log(1/0.23)) / 4
(approximatively).

Note: You can't have a N(0.2,0.03^2) prior on the variance, since it
has to be non-negative.

When dealing with transformations, often the quantiles are a nicer
tool to work with than any specific parameterisation.

Finn

So, we are virtually certain the value is not zero, but also that it is not particularly large. We want the prior to reflect both parts of this information.
>
> First, am I correct that the pc.prior on the precision would not be a good choice for this application, because (a) it specifically sets only a (soft) ceiling, and (b) the only available floor is zero?
>
> Second, if we want to set a different prior that does reflect this a priori knowledge, say N(.2, .03), how do we account for the fact that the prior apparently needs to be specified on the *log* precision? As such, I assume it is not as simple as taking the reciprocal of the square of the SD. Once I figure out the log transformation portion, hopefully some normal or truncated normal would work fine for this prior as a practical matter, although perhaps there are other options worth considering.

messages.subject: Group means and spatial confounding
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm fitting a relatively standard varying coefficient model for individual i and region j as

Y_ij = alpha_j + beta_j * X_ij + error_ij

Here, alpha_j = \gamma_0 + error_alpha_j. The "slopes" (beta's) are fit similarly.

There's a well known issue with random effect models like this where one has to assume that error_alpha_j is uncorrelated with X_ij. One fix is to calculate group means, xbar_j and incorporate them into the level 2 model as,

alpha_j  = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 * xbar_j + error_alpha_j

This makes error_alpha_j (mostly) independent of the covariate as it has already adjusted for X via the group mean. Similar adjustments can be made for slopes.

My question is whether or not this adjustment works for spatially smoothed error_alpha_j, say iCAR, models as well. Would such group mean adjustments aid in reducing bias from spatial confounding?

Thanks, and I apologize in advance if I wrote anything silly and illogical!

John

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Group means and spatial confounding
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

neither silly nor illogical, but very tricky...

How to handle spatial confounding in specific situations is largely an
unsolved problem, but it strikes me that your setup isn't entirely
unlike the Spatial+ method (look for recent paper by Dupont et al).
In your context, you're "smoothing" x onto the regions by plain
averaging. In the Spatial+ context then I think the "correct" thing to
do would then to also modify the beta_j * X_ij term to be
beta_j * (X_ij - xbar_j).
The Spatial+ method was derived for a specific smoothing context in a
frequentist setting, and it's not entirely clear what the "correct"
Bayesian analogue is, but your approach, modified by using the
covariate residuals with beta_j, at least seems like plausible
approach to me.

Finn

On Sun, 12 Feb 2023 at 17:59, John T Molitor <moli...@oregonstate.edu> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I'm fitting a relatively standard varying coefficient model for individual i and region j as
>
> Y_ij = alpha_j + beta_j * X_ij + error_ij
>
> Here, alpha_j = \gamma_0 + error_alpha_j. The "slopes" (beta's) are fit similarly.
>
> There's a well known issue with random effect models like this where one has to assume that error_alpha_j is uncorrelated with X_ij. One fix is to calculate group means, xbar_j and incorporate them into the level 2 model as,
>
> alpha_j  = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 * xbar_j + error_alpha_j
>
> This makes error_alpha_j (mostly) independent of the covariate as it has already adjusted for X via the group mean. Similar adjustments can be made for slopes.
>
> My question is whether or not this adjustment works for spatially smoothed error_alpha_j, say iCAR, models as well. Would such group mean adjustments aid in reducing bias from spatial confounding?
>
> Thanks, and I apologize in advance if I wrote anything silly and illogical!
>
> John
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi again Ian,

I've thought of an approach that doesn't require any extra feature
implementation: The component input for model="fixed" is really a
sparse Matrix; the formula feature is just a way to avoid having to
call model.Matrix explicitly.
But for your use case for family="cp", one can instead replace the
input by a code block (or a function call) that handles it instead,
and evaluates the spatial covariates before calling model.Matrix:

my_model_matrix <- function(where) {
  df <- data.frame(
    cov1 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov1"),
    cov2 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov2"),
    cov3 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov3")
  )
  MatrixModels::model.Matrix(~ -1 + cov1 + cov2 + cov3 + cov1:cov2 +
cov1:cov3 + cov2:cov3, data = df)
}

comp <- ~ ... + mix(my_model_matrix(where = .data.), model = "fixed")

Finn

> intended.
> But for "cp" models, this use case wasn't really anticipated, and to
> support automation, it might require a new method for accessing
> spatial covariates may be needed.
> I have an idea for it but will need time to consider it properly.
>
> Currently, inlabru supports things like
>   comp(covariate_raster, ..., main_layer = "name")
> which ends up being evaluated as
>   eval_spatial(covariate_raster, where = .data., layer = main_layer)
> so it gets evaluated at the locations indicated by .data., which
> includes the internal integration points.
> But for
>   comp(~ covar_name)
> it just runs
>   Matrix::Models::model.Matrix(~ covar_name, data = .data.)
>
> So to handle your use case, it doesn't know how to set up the
> likelihood automatically, as you don't know in advance where it will
> want to evaluate the covariates.
> This is nearly only a problem for model="fixed", and for spatial
> covariates you could define new covariate rasters for the product
> interactions and use as regular plain linear covariates instead,
> so I'd suggest that as a workaround.
> Instead of
>   comp(~ -1 + a + b + a:b, model="fixed")
> you'd need to do (if both a and b are layers in a covar raster):
>   covar$ab <- covar$a * covar$b
> (or something like that; it will be different for factor covariates;
> make those into 0/1 dummy variables instead)
> and in the components:
>  ~ a(covar, main_layer="a") + b(covar, main_layer="b") + ab(covar,
> main_layer="ab")
>

Hi Finn,

Thank you! And thank you for your previous reply as well; your responses have been very helpful.

One thing I discovered today with the INLA package that I thought you might want to know is that when the inla() call is in a function, I've discovered the call to formula must be defined as a string before using as.formula(). Otherwise, INLA fails because it can't find the spde object despite it being created within the nested function. Attached is a reproducible example (the data path should be set to use the .Rdata file I attached in my first message in this thread). I'm not sure this is meant to be the behavior, because when I run the steps of the function line by line, inla() will run successfully regardless of how the formula is defined.

Thanks!

Ian

On Monday, February 13, 2023 at 4:05:04 PM UTC-5 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi again Ian,
>
> I've thought of an approach that doesn't require any extra feature
> implementation: The component input for model="fixed" is really a
> sparse Matrix; the formula feature is just a way to avoid having to
> call model.Matrix explicitly.
> But for your use case for family="cp", one can instead replace the
> input by a code block (or a function call) that handles it instead,
> and evaluates the spatial covariates before calling model.Matrix:
>
> my_model_matrix <- function(where) {
> df <- data.frame(
> cov1 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov1"),
> cov2 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov2"),
> cov3 = eval_spatial(covar, where, layer = "cov3")
> )
> MatrixModels::model.Matrix(~ -1 + cov1 + cov2 + cov3 + cov1:cov2 +
> cov1:cov3 + cov2:cov3, data = df)
> }
>
> comp <- ~ ... + mix(my_model_matrix(where = .data.), model = "fixed")
>
>
> Finn
>
> On Fri, 10 Feb 2023 at 15:39, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > you seem to have dropped the ~ - 1 part of the "fixed" component
> > input, you correctly had mix(~ -1 + ...) before.
> > However, before you only used it in the georeferenced part of the
> > model, where MatrixModels::model.Matrix(formula,data=.data.) works as
> > intended.
> > But for "cp" models, this use case wasn't really anticipated, and to
> > support automation, it might require a new method for accessing
> > spatial covariates may be needed.
> > I have an idea for it but will need time to consider it properly.
> >
> > Currently, inlabru supports things like
> > comp(covariate_raster, ..., main_layer = "name")
> > which ends up being evaluated as
> > eval_spatial(covariate_raster, where = .data., layer = main_layer)
> > so it gets evaluated at the locations indicated by .data., which
> > includes the internal integration points.
> > But for
> > comp(~ covar_name)
> > it just runs
> > Matrix::Models::model.Matrix(~ covar_name, data = .data.)
> >
> > So to handle your use case, it doesn't know how to set up the
> > likelihood automatically, as you don't know in advance where it will
> > want to evaluate the covariates.
> > This is nearly only a problem for model="fixed", and for spatial
> > covariates you could define new covariate rasters for the product
> > interactions and use as regular plain linear covariates instead,
> > so I'd suggest that as a workaround.
> > Instead of
> > comp(~ -1 + a + b + a:b, model="fixed")
> > you'd need to do (if both a and b are layers in a covar raster):
> > covar$ab <- covar$a * covar$b
> > (or something like that; it will be different for factor covariates;
> > make those into 0/1 dummy variables instead)
> > and in the components:
> > ~ a(covar, main_layer="a") + b(covar, main_layer="b") + ab(covar,
> > main_layer="ab")
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Fri, 10 Feb 2023 at 15:18, 'Ian McGregor' via R-inla discussion
> > group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Finn,
> > >
> > > Thank you so much for your replies! I have a couple follow-up questions:
> > >
> > > Follow-up 1: inlabru
> > > For inlabru, I changed the code structure to what you suggested, and I added in the samplers argument. Although the code runs, I get the error below, even after trying different implementations of the intercept in the formula (e.g. adding in + max(1) as the warning message suggests). A new version of the code is attached (includes the building the of the border for the samplers argument).
> > >
> > > Warning in add_mapper(component$main, label = component$label, lhoods = lh, :
> > > All covariate evaluations for 'mix' are NULL; an intercept component was likely intended.
> > > Implicit latent intercept component specification is deprecated since version 2.1.14.
> > > Use explicit notation '+ mix(1)' instead.
> > >
> > > Follow-up 2: inla
> > > Thank you for your suggestion about the mesh. I tried changing it to have a resolution of 10 km, though I am finding the same result where running the INLA with 2000 sample points is successful, though running it with all data points (~5.9 million) causes a crash. I'm not sure how to proceed with this, but here is a google drive link with 5 components. I will note that I'm running the full dataset on our computing cluster for speed, but this will run on my normal laptop.
> > > 1) covarsExtract.csv = the full dataset
> > > 2) inlaSubsetErrors = error messages when running INLA for the subset 2000 data points
> > > 3) inlaFullErrors = error messages when running INLA for the full prediction data
> > > 4) inlaSubsetOut = output messages for the subset data points
> > > 5) inlaFullOut = output messages when using all the prediction data
> > >
> > > Thank you again!
> > >
> > > On Friday, February 10, 2023 at 6:31:58 AM UTC-5 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > >>
> > >> Turns out there wasn't a bug in inlabru, but rather a mistake in the
> > >> model specification.
> > >> The "formula" is a general R expression, so when using the "fixed"
> > >> component construction for covariate interactions, only the name of
> > >> the combined "fixed" effect should be in the formula.
> > >> With that change, the code should run, although the issues around the
> > >> model specification for the "cp" part still apply.
> > >>
> > >> fit <- bru(
> > >> components = as.formula(compAll),
> > >> inlabru::like(
> > >> formula = coordinates ~ mySmooth,
> > >> family = "cp",
> > >> data = coordDF,
> > >> domain = list(coordinates=mesh),
> > >> include = c("mySmooth")
> > >> ),
> > >> inlabru::like(
> > >> formula = dist ~ Intercept + mix,
> > >> family = "binomial",
> > >> data = as.data.frame(covars),
> > >> exclude = c("mySmooth")
> > >> ),
> > >> options = list(
> > >> control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
> > >> control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")
> > >> )
> > >> )
> > >>
> > >> To help inlabru know it's a linear predictor, use ~ . and make sure
> > >> the include/exclude info is correct:
> > >> fit <- bru(
> > >> components = as.formula(compAll),
> > >> inlabru::like(
> > >> formula = coordinates ~ .,
> > >> family = "cp",
> > >> data = coordDF,
> > >> domain = list(coordinates=mesh),
> > >> include = c("mySmooth")
> > >> ),
> > >> inlabru::like(
> > >> formula = dist ~ .,
> > >> family = "binomial",
> > >> data = as.data.frame(covars),
> > >> exclude = c("mySmooth")
> > >> ),
> > >> options = list(
> > >> control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
> > >> control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")
> > >> )
> > >> )
> > >>
> > >> Finn
> > >>
> > >> On Fri, 10 Feb 2023 at 10:50, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >> >
> > >> > Hi,
> > >> >
> > >> > 1. To the extent that such model selection would be appropriate in a
> > >> > frequentistic GLM setting, it would also be reasonable in a Bayesian
> > >> > GLM setting. From what I read nowadays it's a bit frowned upon also
> > >> > in "standard" GLM settings (especially stepwise selection is very much
> > >> > frowned upon). But there are variations on these methods that can be
> > >> > sensible in predictions settings where parameter inference isn't of
> > >> > interest; keeping more covariates is only a problem if it makes
> > >> > prediction worse. But to assess prediction fairly you'd need a
> > >> > sensibly designed cross-validation approach, for example. How to do
> > >> > this appropriately is really an open research problem, and this isn't
> > >> > tied to INLA, that just provides the calculations. It applies to _all_
> > >> > spatial models.
> > >> >
> > >> > 2. Your prediction grid resolution shouldn't dictate your random field
> > >> > component mesh resolution. The model mesh resolution only need to be
> > >> > able to capture the spatial correlation; if that's estimated to ~100,
> > >> > then the mesh resolution should be ok with being ~10.
> > >> >
> > >> > 3. In the inlabru code you don't just have a presence/absence Binomial
> > >> > model, but also an LGCP likelihood, but there are no common components
> > >> > between the two likelihoods, so it's unclear what the goal is. You're
> > >> > also missing the samplers= argument, which makes it try to build a
> > >> > model across the whole mesh, which is bound to be problematic when the
> > >> > points onely cover parts of the domain.
> > >> > If the fine resolution covariates had been involved, you'd have the
> > >> > issue of needing an integration scheme fine enough to capture the
> > >> > covariate values, and that's I guess where your idea of needing a very
> > >> > fine mesh came from, although that would have needed to be applied to
> > >> > the max.edge value, not the cutoff. However, that's unlikely to be
> > >> > practical.
> > >> > We have an ongoing research project on how to better deal with such
> > >> > high resolution covariates for lgcp models.
> > >> > For now, a better/safer approach is to smooth the covariates onto e.g.
> > >> > the mesh used for the mySmooth model; local weighted averaging in some
> > >> > form.
> > >> >
> > >> > But for 3, I removed the lgcp part of the model and stepped into the
> > >> > inlabru code, and there does appear to be some actual bug as well,
> > >> > related to the "fixed" model, as somehow the entire model A-matrix has
> > >> > become zero. I'll investigate.
> > >> >
> > >> > Finn
> > >> >
> > >> >
> > >> > On Thu, 9 Feb 2023 at 20:50, 'Ian McGregor' via R-inla discussion
> > >> > group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > >> > >
> > >> > > Hi,
> > >> > >
> > >> > > Context: I have presence-absence data over a large spatial area. In a non-spatial glm, my goal was to predict the probability of presence based on a number of geographical covariates. Once I had the "best" model after model selection, I would then use the resultant equation to predict the probability over a very fine grid located in a small portion of the original spatial area.
> > >> > >
> > >> > > As my residuals had large spatial autocorrelation, I turned to INLA. However, I've been having issues with comprehension. I have three main questions:
> > >> > >
> > >> > > 1. Model selection
> > >> > >
> > >> > > In standard GLM statistics, I would fit a model with fixed effects and the most probable interactions, then compare AIC and iteratively remove covariates until I have the best model. Then, I would use the final one to predict over a new area.
> > >> > > I had assumed this would be the case for INLA, but I am not sure. For example, I have INLA code that runs and successfully runs for the observation data. I then removed covariates and compared WAIC, and determined my "best" model.
> > >> > > Main question: Should I be following the standard model selection procedure for INLA in this way? Or does the inclusion of a prediction matrix mean I don't have to?
> > >> > >
> > >> > > 2. Observation data vs prediction data
> > >> > >
> > >> > > My observational data is spread out over a very large spatial area (all of northern Myanmar), with ~5500 points (10:1 ratio of absence : presence). However, my prediction data is on a much finer grid. Specifically, it is 10 m resolution with 5.9 million pixels. I have the geographical covariate values for all the observational data points plus all the grid pixels.
> > >> > > To account for this, I ensured the mesh had a low cut-off (0.01), because 0.01 km = 10 m.
> > >> > > When trying to run INLA with the full prediction data, INLA would crash and say "Rerun with better starting values." I tried specifying pcmatern mesh and priors, but that did not work.
> > >> > > However, when I tried using only a sample of the prediction data (2000 pixels vs all 5.9 million), the INLA run was successful.
> > >> > > Main question: Is the size difference between my observational data and prediction data contributing to INLA's crashing? It appears to be so.
> > >> > >
> > >> > > 3. inlabru
> > >> > >
> > >> > > I had tried using inlabru because I thought that might help the crashing issues I was experiencing earlier. However, I found that when trying to use inlabru on just the observational data, it always crashes. I have included the code in the code snippet.
> > >> > > I thought I had translated the INLA code correctly to inlabru based on the vignettes and what I could understand from them.
> > >> > > Main question: Is there something I'm missing from the inlabru version of the code?
> > >> > >
> > >> > >
> > >> > > 3. Code

> > >> > > Thank you so much for your help / advice. This is very appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Group means and spatial confounding
messages.body_plain:
this confounding thing might be one of those that we have to learn to
live with. I would check this one, which is a recent, and pretty good,
review of the topic

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.05743.pdf

On Sun, 2023-02-12 at 09:59 -0800, John T Molitor wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I'm fitting a relatively standard varying coefficient model for
> individual i and region j as
>
> Y_ij = alpha_j + beta_j * X_ij + error_ij
>
> Here, alpha_j = \gamma_0 + error_alpha_j. The "slopes" (beta's) are
> fit similarly.
>
> There's a well known issue with random effect models like this where
> one has to assume that error_alpha_j is uncorrelated with X_ij. One
> fix is to calculate group means, xbar_j and incorporate them into the
> level 2 model as,
>
> alpha_j  = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 * xbar_j + error_alpha_j
>
> This makes error_alpha_j (mostly) independent of the covariate as it
> has already adjusted for X via the group mean. Similar adjustments can
> be made for slopes.
>
> My question is whether or not this adjustment works for spatially
> smoothed error_alpha_j, say iCAR, models as well. Would such group
> mean adjustments aid in reducing bias from spatial confounding?
>
> Thanks, and I apologize in advance if I wrote anything silly and
> illogical!
>
> John

Thank you for the help,
Alessandro

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Summary of the implemented priors
messages.body_plain:
The bru objects are inla objects with some extra added information, so all methods that extract info from inla objects should work on bru objects.

There were a couple of bugs in the inla package until not long ago that meant it didn’t always detect inla objects correctly, but that has been fixed, so if it complains, upgrade inla and try again.

Finn

messages.subject: Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
messages.subject_clean: Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm an INLA newbie, and could use some help trying to create an SPDE model for high-dimension data.  All of the examples I've seen have been strictly 2D spatial models, however the problem I'm working on needs a minimum of 5, possibly 7 dimensions in the spatial analysis.

A toy example is trying to build a mesh over a combination of position and velocity:

n = 1000
x = rnorm(n)
y = rnorm(n)
z = rnorm(n)
vx = rnorm(n)
vy = rnorm(n)
vz = rnorm(n)
mesh.6d <- inla.mesh.create(cbind(x,y,z,vx,vy,vz))

This fails with the error:
fmesher.cc(567) Points not in the plane or on a sphere, and triangulation empty.
meshc.cc(1359)  NOT IMPLEMENTED: bool fmesh::MeshC::CET(int, double)

I've been unable to find examples or documentation for building models in higher dimensions, so I don't know what options are available.  Does anyone have experience building SPDE models in dimension >3?

Best,
Jason Bates

This is due to a fundamental problem with the inla.group-workaround, in that it needs to be applied simultaneously to _all_ the covariate values to work as intended (in the current code you apply it separately for the estimation and prediction values).  A better (in my opinion) solution is to use a proper basis function representation of the smooth effect.  This can be achieved by replacing the "rw2" model with a 1D spde model (with fixed long range).  I don't have a good working example of this at hand, but 1D spde examples are available here:
> > > > > > > > > > > > >   http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss
> > > > > > > > > > > > > See the Tokyo example, with "free" boundary conditions instead of cyclic. degree=2 gives piecewise quadratic basis functions, which plays well the alpha=2 1D spde model.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > This decouples the covariate values from the representation of the smooth effect, which mostly eliminates the "observations too close" problem.

knots<-seq(min(dat1$depth.std, na.rm = T) - 1,

                       degree = 2, boundary = "free", alpha=2)

A_dep <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh1d, dat1$depth.std)

spde_dep <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh1d,
                              prior.range = c(5, NA),

"Error in qr.coef(a, b) : 'qr' and 'y' must have the same number of rows"

the inla.spde2.matern function only runs if I remove the prior.range argument, do you have any thoughts on what is causing that problem?

Thanks again,

Sylvan

This is due to a fundamental problem with the inla.group-workaround, in that it needs to be applied simultaneously to _all_ the covariate values to work as intended (in the current code you apply it separately for the estimation and prediction values).  A better (in my opinion) solution is to use a proper basis function representation of the smooth effect.  This can be achieved by replacing the "rw2" model with a 1D spde model (with fixed long range).  I don't have a good working example of this at hand, but 1D spde examples are available here:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >   http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > See the Tokyo example, with "free" boundary conditions instead of cyclic. degree=2 gives piecewise quadratic basis functions, which plays well the alpha=2 1D spde model.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > This decouples the covariate values from the representation of the smooth effect, which mostly eliminates the "observations too close" problem.
