messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] GRF approximation
messages.body_plain:
Since you use Q=Q_T x Q_s, you are using a tensor product space-time
basis, with each \psi_j(s,t) being the product of a spatial basis
function and a temporal basis function,
and you impose a product-separable precision/covariance structure on
the process.
Assuming you're basing the model on Markov models in both space and
time, then your space-time process is Markov both in the continuous
domain and with respect to the basis weights, assuming the temporal
basis functions are also local in time.
With non-local basis functions, the Markov property would only hold
with respect to a graph with a dense set of edges, which usually isn't
called Markov (even though strictly speaking it is; the Markov
property is always expressed in relation to some "neighbourhood
system/topology")

So your \tilde{z} vector is a discrete domain GMRF, but the underlying
infinite/continuous domain SPDE is also a GMRF with respect to the
continuous domain; when the SPDE operator is of integer order, a
continuous Markov property holds.

The finite dimensional sum psi_j(s,t) z_j expression isn't quite the
full SPDE process, but rather a finite rank approximation of it.
However, that's _also_ a Markov process here; it's piecewise
conditionally deterministic.

The class of GMRF models is just a subset of GRF processes; _Every_
GMRF is a GRF.
Some of the literature is a bit confused on this point, and we didn't
even have the full picture in the 2011 SPDE/GRMF paper. The full
theory can be found in the books/papers by Rozanov (1970s/ early 80s).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] GRF approximation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

"In my equation (3) z_t is assumed to be a spatio-temporal GF with
AR(1) dynamics which are represented in eq. (4).
Why do I model these "innovations" w_t with a purely spatial Matern
covariance? What are innovations?"

The short answer is "because it's convenient/easy to construct that model".
In any AR(1) model we write
  z_{t+1} = a z_t + w_t
and w_t are sometimes called "innovations" because they describe
what's "new", after taking the scaled version "a z_t" of "z_t".
In the spatial setting, we need a spatial model for these w_t fields,
and since we know how to construct Matern fields, that's just an easy
choice to make.

Because of the "separable" nature of the AR(1) space-time model, we
can take the regular AR(1) 1-dim "time" Q_T precision, and the spatial
Q_S precision (from the spatial Matern model), and get the space-time
precision as
Q_T \otimes Q_S.

The B in B\xi_t is the observation model matrix, yes. It contains the
evaluated product-basis functions for the space-time basis, at the
observation locations.

Finn

>
> The short answer is "because it's convenient/easy to construct that model".
> In any AR(1) model we write
> z_{t+1} = a z_t + w_t
> and w_t are sometimes called "innovations" because they describe
> what's "new", after taking the scaled version "a z_t" of "z_t".
> In the spatial setting, we need a spatial model for these w_t fields,
> and since we know how to construct Matern fields, that's just an easy
> choice to make.
>
> Because of the "separable" nature of the AR(1) space-time model, we
> can take the regular AR(1) 1-dim "time" Q_T precision, and the spatial
> Q_S precision (from the spatial Matern model), and get the space-time
> precision as
> Q_T \otimes Q_S.

> evaluated product-basis functions for the space-time basis, at the
> observation locations.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Group means and spatial confounding
messages.body_plain:
The model you suggested (with beta_W*xbar_j and deviance beta_j*(x_ij-xbar_j)) is very robust to inclusion/exclusion of spatially smoothed intercept terms ("bym2"). Addition of the intercept-level smoothed terms yields smoothed results, while the "iid" intercept-level errors produce "patchy" results, while the overall pattern is the same. This is not true for simpler models!

However, I would like to reconstruct what would be obtained in the "original" model, without the beta_W*xbar_j term, and only with beta_j * X_ij. It seems that I have to take the beta_j from the deviance model and add in intercept-level residuals to get the beta_j I would have gotten in the original model, but without spatial confounding.

Does this make sense? Any thoughts would be appreciated.

John

On Monday, February 13, 2023 at 8:57:25 AM UTC-8 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi,
>
> neither silly nor illogical, but very tricky...
>
> How to handle spatial confounding in specific situations is largely an
> unsolved problem, but it strikes me that your setup isn't entirely
> unlike the Spatial+ method (look for recent paper by Dupont et al).
> In your context, you're "smoothing" x onto the regions by plain
> averaging. In the Spatial+ context then I think the "correct" thing to
> do would then to also modify the beta_j * X_ij term to be
> beta_j * (X_ij - xbar_j).
> The Spatial+ method was derived for a specific smoothing context in a
> frequentist setting, and it's not entirely clear what the "correct"
> Bayesian analogue is, but your approach, modified by using the
> covariate residuals with beta_j, at least seems like plausible
> approach to me.
>
> Finn
>
> On Sun, 12 Feb 2023 at 17:59, John T Molitor <moli...@oregonstate.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I'm fitting a relatively standard varying coefficient model for individual i and region j as
> >
> > Y_ij = alpha_j + beta_j * X_ij + error_ij
> >
> > Here, alpha_j = \gamma_0 + error_alpha_j. The "slopes" (beta's) are fit similarly.
> >
> > There's a well known issue with random effect models like this where one has to assume that error_alpha_j is uncorrelated with X_ij. One fix is to calculate group means, xbar_j and incorporate them into the level 2 model as,
> >
> > alpha_j = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 * xbar_j + error_alpha_j
> >
> > This makes error_alpha_j (mostly) independent of the covariate as it has already adjusted for X via the group mean. Similar adjustments can be made for slopes.
> >
> > My question is whether or not this adjustment works for spatially smoothed error_alpha_j, say iCAR, models as well. Would such group mean adjustments aid in reducing bias from spatial confounding?
> >
> > Thanks, and I apologize in advance if I wrote anything silly and illogical!
> >
> > John

messages.subject: Plots of population-level predictions from a random coefficients GLMM
messages.subject_clean: Plots of population-level predictions from a random coefficients GLMM
messages.body_plain:
I trying to fit a logistic regression model with random coefficients. I don't have any trouble fitting the model but I'm interested in producing plots that show, for example, predicted y over the range of precipitation in the data. I can produce prediction curves by incorporating extra rows in the data (where y=NA, as explained at r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>), but as far as I can tell, that requires you to include values for the random effects, so essentially you produce a line for each level of the random effect.

While that's useful, I'm also interested in plotting the population-level effect (from just the fixed effect with credible intervals). I'm not a trained statistician, so I apologize if I missed it, but I haven't been able to figure out how to do this. I'm ultimately hoping to have graphs that show both the variability in the random coefficients but also show the population-level effect.

I included a dummy example below to show what I've done so far, including a data frame that can be used to generate predictions for one level of the random effect. You can potentially manually calculate the mean population-level effect (as shown below), but that of course does not include any measure of error. I would appreciate any suggestions for how to generate plots of the population-level predictions (not just plots of the fixed effect coefficients as seems the default in INLA). Thanks!

# generate data
n.groups <- 16
n.years <- 10
n <- n.groups * n.years
pop <- gl(n = n.groups, k = n.years)

prec <- runif(n, 0, 1)
N <- round(runif(n, 10, 50) )
Xmat <- model.matrix(~pop*prec-1-prec)

intercept.mean <- 1 # Select hyperparams
intercept.sd <http://intercept.sd> <- 1
slope.mean <- -2
slope.sd <http://slope.sd> <- 1
intercept.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=intercept.mean, sd=intercept.sd <http://intercept.sd>)
slope.effects <- rnorm(n=n.groups, mean=slope.mean, sd=slope.sd <http://slope.sd>)
all.effects <- c(intercept.effects, slope.effects) # Put them all together

lin.pred <- Xmat %*% all.effects # Value of lin.predictor
exp.p <- exp(lin.pred) / (1 + exp(lin.pred)) # Expected proportion
C <- rbinom(n=n, size=N, prob=exp.p) # Add binomial variation

# compile data
occ.data <- data.frame(pop = rep(as.numeric(pop), C),
                       pop1 = rep(as.numeric(pop), C),
                       prec = rep(prec, C),
                       y = 1)
unocc.data <- data.frame(pop = rep(as.numeric(pop), N-C),
                       pop1 = rep(as.numeric(pop), N-C),
                       prec = rep(as.numeric(prec), N-C),
                       y = 0)
data <- rbind(occ.data, unocc.data)

# run model
form <- formula(y ~ prec + f(pop, model = "iid", hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1e-06), fixed = TRUE))) +
                  f(pop1, prec, values = 1:56, model = "iid", hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = F, prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.05)))))
mod <- inla(form, family ="binomial", data=data,
            control.fixed = list(
              mean = 0,
              prec = list(default = 1e-04)),
            control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, config=TRUE))
mod$summary.fixed

# data for predictions for one level of random effect
pred.df <- data.frame(pop=1,
                      pop1 = 1,
                      prec = seq(from=min(data$prec), to=max(data$prec), length=100),
                      y = NA)

# manual calculation for mean population-level effect
prec.vals <- seq(from=min(data$prec), to=max(data$prec), length=100)
output <- boot::inv.logit(mod$summary.fixed$mean[2] * prec.vals)
plot(output ~ prec.vals, type="l")

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Modeling 3D Point Process in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the principle would be the same as for 2D fields, but there is less
direct support for 3D point processes and fields at the moment.
For SPDE/Matern fields in 3D, you can try the experimental
https://github.com/finnlindgren/inlamesh3d package, that takes a given
tetrahedralization (e.g. from delaunayn() on a regular 3D lattice) and
creates a mesh object that can be used with special the special
version of inla.spde2.matern(). It also has an inla.spde.make.A()
function that can be used in the same way as for 2D meshes.
One can use that to construct the point process likelihood in
essentially the same way as for 2D.

The 3D support will be merged into INLA and the upcoming fmesher
package; until then, it's experimental and you'll need to "know what
you're doing" to use it...

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Creating a mesh in higher dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

the fmesher code only supports 2-manifolds (and the R code also
supports 1-manifolds).
There is 3-manifold support with tetrahedral meshes in the
experimental https://github.com/finnlindgren/inlamesh3d package.
There, the package requires the user to create the mesh themselves,
e.g. using delaunayn on a suitable set of points, and the package then
has inla.mesh.fem and inla.spde.make.A methods to work with such
tetrahedral meshes.

In theory, that code could be extended to dim > 3, but the gain of
using sparse FEM representations of the field diminishes with higher
dimensions.

In your 6-dimensional case, one could consider a tensor product basis
between two tetrahedral meshes; one for location and one for velocity;
it should be straightforward to construct such a model with precision
kronecker products and inla.generic(), but I suspect the computational
cost wouldn't be worth it.  If you do try it, I strongly recommend
_not_ using observed locations as seed points for the mesh; consider a
quasi-regular set of points instead, and rely on inla.spde.make.A to
make the link between basis functions and observation locations.
Data-seeded irregular meshes can be computationally deficient, leading
to singular matrices etc (which is why the "cutoff" argument to
inla.spde.2d() exists, to prevent direct use of arbitrarily close
points).

Finn

messages.subject: Why do two Zero-Inflated Poisson models that fit the same data but in different ways with INLA, estimate the parameters differently?
messages.subject_clean: Why do two Zero-Inflated Poisson models that fit the same data but in different ways with INLA, estimate the parameters differently?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!
I am trying to fit a ZIP model using INLA with two linear predictors, one for the binomial part, and another one for the Poisson part. I have tried to fit the simplest model (just intercept in both cases). We have conducted it in two different ways:
- (M1) I fit a model with the Zero-Inflated Poisson family that INLA has by default ("zeroinflatedpoisson1"), and
- (M2) I fit it as a joint likelihood using a binomial and a ZIP families (following the advanced example in the documentation).
Both models fit the same ZIP simulated data. The point is that results are different for the binomial part and I was wondering why in the case of the joint likelihood is not working as I was expecting.
I attach a Rmd and a HTML with the developed code in case it is helpful.
Many thanks!
Oihane.
